title: Callo: Serving Cache-Miss Requests with Speculative Decoding on Invalidated KV under Prefill-Decode Disaggregation
summary: Agent sessions may involve frequent context edits, which effectively invalidate cached KV state and force requests to wait for re-prefill before decoding. We present Callo, a disaggregated serving system that leverages invalidated KV for speculative drafts to reduce this latency, while verifying drafts against the exact KV after prefill before committing tokens. Callo makes effective use of decode resources by scheduling speculations during periods of underutilization and preempting speculations when drafts are likely to not be accepted. We evaluated Callo on a two-GPU testbed using SWE-agent sessions across three model families, observing all-request speedups of 1.05-1.19x over vLLM at moderate load. We demonstrate that these gains are also realized at scale through cluster-level simulations driven by real-world traces.

title: When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support
summary: Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support, a lightweight extension of a propose--simulate--refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone.These results characterize a reliability--coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.

title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
summary: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

title: HerAgent: A Block-Level Checkpointing Harness for Coding-Agent Environment Setup
summary: Modern coding agents rely on establishing executable software environments before they can perform software engineering tasks such as testing, debugging, and patch validation. Existing setup agents typically control progress at either single-command or whole-script granularity, making recovery either too local to remove polluted state or too coarse to preserve useful progress. HerAgent's main contribution is semantic setup blocks: a single progress-control abstraction used for execution, validation, checkpointing, repair, and rollback. title: CANTraj: Recovering Vehicle Trajectories from CAN Signals in Naturalistic Driving
summary: Open driving releases and usage-based insurance programs often claim to prevent privacy breaches by omitting GPS records when sharing or collecting vehicle data. However, removing GPS coordinates from driving logs does not erase the location information carried by vehicle signals. While prior route-inference attacks have demonstrated that speed, steering, and driving events can be matched to road networks to reconstruct trajectories, existing studies rely on inconsistent prior assumptions and evaluation metrics and are tested only on small, restricted datasets, making their results difficult to compare and their real-world effectiveness uncertain. We release CANTraj, a naturalistic driving dataset pairing decoded CAN events with time-aligned GNSS trajectories (3,940 drives, 454 drivers), and CANTraj-Bench for evaluating trajectory recovery (3,675 drives, 431 drivers, 1,380 hours, 85,919 km). On 776 evaluation drives from 94 unseen drivers, we compare six re-implemented attacks and benchmark baselines under explicit information-access protocols, paired comparisons, and metrics incorporating failures. Experiments show that combining steering signals with road-network constraints yields the largest gain: With a known start and heading, adding steering to speed raises the online map filter's five-minute route recovery from 56% to 87%, with a median average displacement error of 43 m versus 921 m for map-free dead reckoning. Offline beam search recovers 88% of test routes with the heading and 81% without it. Because methods fail on different windows, we also evaluate an LLM harness that selects among candidate routes on 659 five-minute windows; its best configuration recovers 79% of routes on test and 83% on few-shot, outperforming the best baseline on test and matching it on few-shot. title: Efficiency Gains in Social Science Research: A Prospective Silicon Sampling Protocol for Pre-Treatment and Code Optimization
summary: This study evaluates the methodological potential of using large language models (LLMs) to generate synthetic datasets prior to real-world data collection, thereby streamlining subsequent processing and statistical analysis. title: LECAT: Measuring LLM Category Learning from Pretraining Data
summary: Humans know that airplanes are fast, that this extends to red airplanes, but that it does not hold for broken airplanes. How do LLMs acquire category knowledge that humans learn and apply effortlessly? We introduce LeCat, a two-part framework to analyze LLM's Learning of Category knowledge. First, we use LeCat to evaluate models on their ability to learn category knowledge, distinguishing between three cases: memorization of in-domain category knowledge, generalization to unseen instances, and ability to flexibly use knowledge in appropriate contexts. Then, we use LeCat to trace how this knowledge can be learned in pretraining from text that may encode category knowledge in various ways, such as verbatim repetition or exceptions, which we refer to as forms of "knowledge expression". We first assess open-source pretrained models using 199 curated category-feature pairs and analyze their training data. Our findings suggest that strengthening context and category-feature co-occurrence likelihood (PMI) improve learning for larger models and verbatim rule-like statements diminish flexible category learning. To systematically isolate these effects, we then train a 68M model from scratch with precise control over the categorical information each sees in their training data, confirming that verbatim repetition reduces flexible learning but mixture of diverse knowledge expressions lead to more robust category learning. Together, our findings highlight that while contextual flexibility is persistently difficult for models, how category knowledge is expressed in pretraining greatly impacts models' acquisition of robust category knowledge.

title: CoPre-MoE: Consolidating and Preserving MoE for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
summary: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.

title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
summary: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
summary:
Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late.
  We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Voice-Based Conversational Agents as AI Care Assistants: Evaluating Personalization, Intervention Delivery Fidelity, and Privacy Expectations in Older Adults' Care
summary: Generative AI enables voice-based conversational agents to play more active roles in older adults' care, including personalizing support and operating alongside clinicians and care partners. title: Vision-Language-Action Models: A Life-Cycle Survey of Design, Training and Deployment
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt web-pretrained vision-language models to output robot actions, so that web knowledge carries over to physical control. In under 4 years the field has moved from RT-2, the first VLA, to open models that fine-tune on a single consumer GPU and to proprietary generalists that clean unseen homes. This survey reviews 88 works from December 2022 to October 2026, mainly on manipulation and navigation, plus humanoid control, world-action models and evaluation. We follow a VLA through its life cycle, from model design to training and deployment, along seven axes. Model design covers (a) inputs and memory, what the model observes; (b) architecture, how its pipeline is built; (c) action output, how it produces motor commands; and (d) intermediate predictions, what else it predicts, from reasoning steps to future observations. Training covers (e) pretraining data, the mix of robot, web, human and simulated data, and (f) post-training, adaptation to the target robot. Deployment covers (g) real-time execution, keeping pace with the robot. We analyse 22 models on these axes and report their training data, model size, inference speed and hardware. Three trends emerge: (i) training data has broadened, from about 10,000 hours of teleoperated robot data ($π_0$) to 23,000 community-collected episodes (SmolVLA) and 20,000 hours of egocentric human video (GR00T N1.7); (ii) model sizes have split: most recent models have 3-7 billion parameters, while a new group under one billion runs on consumer GPUs; and (iii) generalist VLAs are emerging that handle both manipulation and navigation, such as UniVLA and Qwen-VLA. We also compare VLAs with world-action models, which predict future observations as well as actions. We review evidence that some VLAs with near-perfect benchmark scores fail when objects or the camera move slightly, and open up further research questions.

title: f-Divergence Self-Play for Tabular Anomaly Detection via Large Language Models
summary: Anomaly detection in tabular data poses significant challenges due to heterogeneous feature types-mixing numerical, categorical, and textual attributes, which complicate learning meaningful representations of normality. Recent work has applied large language models (LLMs) to this problem by serializing table rows as text sequences, yet these approaches rely on one-shot supervised fine-tuning that offers limited signal to tighten the model's description of normality. We propose DiSPaT, a self-play fine-tuning framework that strengthens the model's understanding of normal data. Building on the theoretical foundation of f-divergence minimization, we derive a tight approximation connecting our training objective to reducing the distributional gap between real normal data and model-generated samples. DiSPaT operates through an alternating optimization: at each iteration, the current policy generates synthetic samples that serve as pseudo-anomalies, while a critic discriminator learns to distinguish these from real normal samples; this signal drives policy updates that progressively align the model distribution with the true normal-data distribution. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DiSPaT consistently outperforms prior LLM-based methods, deep learning approaches, and classical unsupervised detectors for tabular anomaly detection.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Null-Space Exploitation in Pseudo-Inverse Control Allocation
summary: Pseudo-inverse methods are widely used to solve control allocation problems for overactuated aircraft with redundant control effectors. These methods reliably satisfy the primary command tracking objective, while the remaining null-space degrees of freedom are in principle available for secondary objectives such as drag reduction or actuator wear balancing. The null-space projector guarantees by construction that primary command tracking remains invariant regardless of the agent output, providing a principled separation between certified primary control and adaptive secondary optimization. The approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear six-degree-of-freedom distributed electric propulsion aircraft model with aero-propulsive effects across diverse mission scenarios, achieving measurable drag reduction compared to the baseline allocation while preserving tracking integrity and respecting actuator constraints. The proposed architecture forms a foundation for future extensions toward multi-objective, mission-conditioned policies.

title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems
summary: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Despite these advances, the community has yet to converge on a shared definition, a reliable evaluation framework, or a research roadmap. We argue that Embodied System 2, realized by a foundation model together with an embodied harness, forms the decision-making core of agentic robotics. Its central challenge is to translate general-purpose reasoning into effective and verifiable actions under physical constraints such as limited reaction time, mechanical limits, unpredictable environment changes, and irreversible consequences. Motivated by this perspective, we propose an evaluation framework that measures both model capabilities and closed-loop system performance. Furthermore, we identify the principles that carry over from digital to physical agents and the challenges that must be addressed to achieve reliable physical autonomy. On top of the Embodied System 2 and the evaluation framework, we envision a research roadmap toward sustained autonomy: the ability to perform work safely and reliably with progressively broader responsibility, from executing individual primitives to fulfilling standing roles.

title: VLAN: Vision-Language Accessible Navigation
summary: Accessible mobility is user-conditioned rather than scene-intrinsic, as walkable paths for one embodiment are inaccessible to another. title: Formulating Uncomputation Beyond Classical Ancilla Use
summary:
Ancilla qubits are routinely used to simplify quantum circuit construction and reduce implementation costs, but their use introduces the burden of designing proper uncomputation afterward. To alleviate this, prior work has developed automated uncomputation synthesis based on a computational-basis formulation of ancilla use. However, this formulation is tailored to classically structured ancilla computations. For more general circuits, it may be undefined, yield unintended functionality, or fail to synthesize uncomputation. It therefore falls short of providing a precise and general formulation of uncomputation beyond classical ancilla use.
  To address these limitations, we propose a new formulation of ancilla use that specifies the operation of each gate through two complementary aspects: (1) the functionality it implements and (2) the transformation it induces on ancilla roles. Based on this specification, we define uncomputation as restoring the initial ancilla role while implementing the identity functionality. This perspective enables a simple Use-first strategy for automatically synthesizing uncomputation in cases both within and beyond the scope of prior approaches. We further develop a complete inference system for reasoning about specifications, together with a derivation-directed procedure for automatically synthesizing efficient uncomputation, enabling systematic uncomputation synthesis even in challenging cases beyond the scope of our automatic strategy.

title: An In-Silico Audit of Topographic Organization in a Multimodal Brain-Response Model
summary: TRIBE v2 (d'Ascoli et al., 2026) predicts fMRI responses across the cortical surface from video, audio and text. Its authors validated it with category-selective localizers (faces, places, bodies, words) and language contrasts, but not with the classic topographic organization of sensory cortex: retinotopy, tonotopy, and motion selectivity in area MT+. There is a clear architectural reason to expect retinotopy to fail: TRIBE's video features are averaged over space before the response head, which should discard visual-field position. I present mapping stimuli, a fitting pipeline adapted from standard fMRI mapping analyses, and a stand-in model with known ground truth that serves as a positive and negative control, and apply them to TRIBE v2's predictions, comparing the fitted maps with human atlases using spin tests. TRIBE v2 shows a sharp split. There is no contralateral hemifield response and no polar-angle map, robustly across stimulus controls. There is no tonotopic gradient in primary auditory cortex: best frequencies span an interquartile range of only 0.14 octaves across core and belt, and the null persists with loudness-equalized tones. An eccentricity-like gradient appears only when the ring geometry changes, consistent with global image statistics rather than a positional code. In contrast, motion selectivity is strong and precisely localized: 22% of the 1% most motion-selective vertices fall in MT+, which covers 0.42% of cortex. In-silico experiments that depend on feature identity appear viable with TRIBE v2, while those that depend on visual-field or frequency position are not supported by the current model.

title: Contagious Fingerprints: When LLMs Inherit Another Model's Identity
summary: The fingerprint by which a classifier recognizes the LLM behind a text is usually treated as a fixed property of the model. We show that it is contagious: a model that continues a conversation begun by another model inherits that model's fingerprint. This undermines audits of API relays, which can serve the first turns of a conversation with the model a customer pays for and silently hand the rest to a cheaper one. After such a handoff, detection of the substitute by a text classifier drops from 0.97 to 0.72 (DeepSeek replacing Claude Sonnet) and from 0.87 to 0.54 for a same-vendor downgrade (Haiku), and retraining on handoff data repairs only substitutes seen in training. Preregistered experiments trace the contagion to imitation of the history's style. History also moves a model away from its own fingerprint: active probes are not camouflaged, but when calibrated on fresh conversations they flag \emph{honest} models on long contexts at rates up to 1.00, and a standard MMD equality test rejects all nine models we test. Both failures come from comparing a history-dependent reply with a history-free reference. We propose \textsc{Lineup}, which samples references from the claimed model \emph{on the same history} and tests the audited reply by its rank among them. \textsc{Lineup} controls false positives by exchangeability and needs no fitted threshold or log-probabilities. With contemporaneous references on two closed models, its false-positive rate is 0.056 (preregistered bound 0.10), and it detects 0.81 of substitute sessions across six pairs after four audited turns.
